newsitem.title: UK: IFC outlines future direction in emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: IFC outlines future direction in emerging markets.

text.p: The International Finance Corporation (IFC), the private finance wing of the World Bank, said its future work in developing countries will focus on mobilising domestic savings and promoting new fund vehicles.

As part of a report on investment funds in emerging markets released this week, the Washington-based IFC said it would help promote pension funds, mutual funds and local pools for venture capital funds as a way of encouraging domestic savings.
"The IFC will also work closely with the World Bank to support pension reforms," the report said.
It will identify technical partners and invest in private pension fund managers in order to help set high standards for pension fund management.

Private equity funds and venture capital funds, particularly in new sectors and new countries would help add depth and liquidity to markets, drawing in new domestic and foreign investors, the IFC said.

For "pre-emerging" markets, which have not yet benefited from foreign portfolio investment, the IFC will help set up portfolio funds to attract capital. The IFC said Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Cambodia were immediate targets.

More sophisticated investors who want access to emerging markets returns but a lower risk profile have been attracted by index funds, and the IFC said it would continue to roll out index funds in more regions.

"As well as promoting specific funds, this work will involve adding new markets to its Emerging Markets Database," the report said. "Indeed, several countries are asking IFC to include them in the coverage, as this ensures automatic foreign portfolio investment from index funds."
The IFC noted that as bond markets in developing countries deepen, there would be opportunities to promote funds investing in private corporate debt.

But it said its efforts would "depend to a significant extent on liberalisation efforts by governments (including those not directly related to funds, such as privatisation and private participation in infrastructure) and investor perceptions."
